value.description: Quillfield Automation LLC is a one-person automation studio in Brooklyn, New York, founded in 2026 by Jordan Ellis. We design and build AI-assisted workflow automations for small professional-services firms: law, accounting, architecture and marketing firms of 5 to 50 staff. We provide three services. The AI Workflow Audit finds the repetitive work worth automating. The Automation Build puts the chosen workflows into daily use. The Automation Care Retainer keeps them running, secure and up to date.
value.mission: To give small professional firms back the hours they lose to repetitive admin. Many small firms spend a large part of each week copying data between tools, chasing documents and writing the same emails again and again. Large consultancies do not serve them, and ready-made AI tools rarely fit how they work. We build reliable, well-documented automations around the tools a firm already uses, so its people can spend their time on client work. This matters because small firms compete on care and expertise, not on admin capacity.
value.positioning: For owners and office managers of small professional-services firms who know automation could help but have no technical staff, Quillfield Automation is a hands-on automation partner in the small-business IT and consulting market. Unlike larger agencies, clients work directly with the person who designs and builds their system, at fixed project prices. Unlike do-it-yourself AI tools, we map the workflow first, build on the firm's existing software, document every step and stay on to maintain it.
value.vision: A future in which every small professional firm can use automation and AI as safely and confidently as a large one. Ten years from now, Quillfield is a trusted name for practical automation among small firms across the north-east United States: a small team of automation specialists, a library of proven and well-documented workflows, and hundreds of client firms whose staff spend their days on skilled work rather than admin. Success means clients who stay for years, recommend us to their peers and never feel locked in.

value.philosophy: We believe technology should serve people's working day, not reshape it around a tool. The best automation is quiet: it removes a chore, works every time and is easy to understand. We would rather automate one workflow well than ten badly. And we believe clients should always own, and understand, what we build for them.
value.values:
1. Clarity over cleverness
2. Reliability in everything we deliver
3. Honesty about what AI can and cannot do
4. Respect for client data and privacy
5. Long-term partnership
value.principles:
1. We map and measure a workflow before we automate it.
2. We quote fixed prices and agree the scope in writing.
3. We build on the client's existing tools wherever we can.
4. Every automation that affects clients or money has a named person who checks it.
5. We document every build so the client could run it without us.
6. We never put client data into a new tool without the client's written approval.
7. We turn down work we cannot deliver well.
value.manifesto: We stand for small firms having the same smart tools as large ones. We stand for automation that people understand, own and trust. We stand against hype, black-box systems and contracts that lock clients in. We stand against software that replaces people's judgement without anyone checking it. Everything we build exists for one reason: to give people back time for the work they chose their profession for.

requirements.name: LLC publication requirement (NY LLC Law, Section 206)
requirements.notes: Notice of formation published once a week for six consecutive weeks in two newspapers (one daily, one weekly) chosen by the Kings County Clerk, within 120 days of formation; the Certificate of Publication, with the publishers' affidavits, is then filed with the Department of State.

requirements.name: Operating Agreement (single-member)
requirements.notes: New York expects an LLC to adopt a written operating agreement within 90 days of filing its Articles of Organization, even with one member.

requirements.name: NYS LLC annual filing fee (Form IT-204-LL)
requirements.reference: First filing due with the 2027 tax year
requirements.notes: A single-member LLC with New York income pays the fee each year. It is $25 while New York gross income stays at or under $100,000 and rises by income band above that; confirm the band each year with the accountant.

requirements.name: New York State sales tax
requirements.notes: Consulting and custom automation services are generally not subject to New York sales tax, so no Certificate of Authority is held. Reselling software licenses or pre-written software would change this. To be confirmed with the accountant.

requirements.name: NYC Unincorporated Business Tax (UBT)
requirements.notes: A single-member LLC doing business in New York City may owe UBT once its business income passes the exemption threshold. To be confirmed with the accountant each year.

expenses.name: NY Articles of Organization filing
expenses.description: Department of State filing fee, paid online at formation.

expenses.name: LLC publication in two Brooklyn newspapers
expenses.description: Six weeks in a daily and a weekly newspaper. Publication costs vary a lot by county in New York City; Kings County quotes ranged from about $900 to $1,500.

expenses.name: Certificate of Publication filing
expenses.description: Department of State fee for filing the Certificate of Publication.

expenses.name: NYS LLC annual filing fee

founders.managementExperience: Led a team of four implementation consultants at the workflow-software company for three years, owning a $600,000 annual services budget and around 40 customer rollouts a year.
achievements: Designed an invoice-intake automation that cut a 30-person accounting firm's processing time by 70% (from 12 to 3.5 hours a week) in 2024
Delivered 120 customer integrations at the workflow-software company, 96% of them on time, 2022–2025

value.teamGaps: As a one-person LLC, Quillfield has no one with a sales and marketing background, no in-house bookkeeping or legal expertise, and no cover for holidays or illness.
value.teamCover: Bookkeeping and taxes are covered by our Brooklyn CPA practice and contracts by a small-business attorney. A freelance automation specialist, trained on our templates, will cover urgent Care Retainer work when Jordan is away, and Jordan meets a SCORE mentor monthly on sales and marketing.

value.aesthetics: A person in their thirties or forties in smart-casual clothes: a navy overshirt or knit over a plain white or light grey top, dark trousers and clean, simple shoes. Few accessories: a plain watch and a laptop in a matte grey sleeve. Neat, practical and unfussy, in navy, teal, off-white and grey. Nothing flashy, and nothing that looks like a tech start-up.
value.attitude-body-language: Calm and attentive. Sits beside the client at the same screen rather than presenting from the front of the room. Open posture, relaxed shoulders and steady eye contact. Listens more than they talk and takes notes by hand. Points to the real workflow on screen when explaining something. Never rushes and never glances at the clock.
value.communication-voice: Plain, precise and friendly. An even tone at a steady pace. Uses the client's own names for their tasks and avoids jargon; when a technical term is needed, it is explained once, in one sentence. Short sentences and concrete numbers: hours saved, steps removed. Honest about limits, and happy to say: "I don't know yet, I'll check." Writes as it speaks: clear subject lines, a summary at the top, then short bullet points.
value.imprint: First impression: "this person understands how our office really works, and won't oversell." Lasting impression: relief and a sense of control. People should feel that their messy processes were taken seriously, that nothing will break without warning, and that they now own a system they understand. They remember the calm, the clear documentation and the hours they got back.

segments.name: Small professional-services firms in New York City

description.business-data: Independent law, accounting, architecture and marketing firms with 5 to 50 staff; partner-owned; no in-house IT or operations engineer; run on Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 plus a practice-management tool.
description.demographics: Decision-makers aged 30 to 60: managing partners, firm founders and operations or office managers, usually college-educated, with annual firm revenue of about $1 million to $10 million.
description.geographics: New York City first, especially Brooklyn and Manhattan, then the wider tri-state area, served remotely with occasional on-site workshops.
description.purchasing: Buy on trust and referrals; spend $5,000 to $30,000 a year on software and outside help; need a clear return in saved hours before committing; prefer a small fixed-price first step and monthly billing for ongoing work.
description.market-size:
Rough estimate: around 12,000 to 15,000 firms of this size in these four professions across the five boroughs. A reachable niche of perhaps 1,000 firms that already use cloud tools and are curious about AI; 20 to 30 clients a year is enough for a solo practice.

Outlook: AI features are moving into the everyday office software these firms already use, and small firms now expect automation to come with it; client-data and AI-use rules are tightening (New York SHIELD Act, bar and CPA guidance), so firms want help that is documented and privacy-reviewed.

profiles.name: The Stretched Operations Manager

description.personal: Dana Morales, 38, operations manager at a 22-person accounting firm in Downtown Brooklyn; the person everyone asks when a system breaks.
description.psychographics: Practical, organized and overloaded; wants fewer manual steps and fewer mistakes; wary of hype and of tools that create more work than they save.
description.hubs: LinkedIn, the firm's software vendor webinars, NYSSCPA events, local chamber of commerce meetups, operations and practice-management Slack groups.
description.habits: Researches on LinkedIn and vendor sites, asks peers for recommendations, needs a written proposal to take to the partners, and prefers a short paid pilot to a big commitment.

profiles.goals: Get hours back each week for the team; make intake, reminders and reporting run on their own; look good to the partners by fixing problems that have lingered for years.
profiles.challenges: Copying data between the practice-management system, email and spreadsheets; chasing clients for documents; no budget for a full-time developer; past tools abandoned after setup.
profiles.objections: Worried about client data privacy and AI mistakes; unsure the savings justify the cost; afraid of being left with automations nobody can fix.

functional: Hand repetitive admin work to reliable automations
Faster client intake and document handling
Automations that keep working after launch
emotional: Confidence that client data is handled safely
social: Be seen by the partners as the person who modernized the firm

profiles.name: The Agency Founder

description.personal: Sam Okafor, 34, founder and creative director of a 9-person marketing agency in Williamsburg.
description.psychographics: Ambitious, curious about AI and quick to try new tools, but short on time to set them up properly; values speed and a professional client experience.
description.hubs: LinkedIn, X, agency founder communities, Brooklyn tech and marketing meetups, podcasts on agency growth.
description.habits: Discovers through LinkedIn posts and founder peers; books a call straight from a website; decides quickly when a case study matches the agency's own problem.

profiles.goals: Grow revenue without growing headcount; deliver client reports and onboarding faster; use AI in a way that holds up in front of clients.
profiles.challenges: Team time lost to reporting, briefs and status updates; a pile of half-connected tools; freelancers who build automations and then disappear.
profiles.objections: Has tried no-code tools alone and hit limits; unsure about paying a consultant for something that might be done in-house; concerned about lock-in.

functional: A clear plan for where AI actually saves time
Scale delivery without hiring more staff
Automations that keep working after launch
emotional: Feel in control of the agency's tools again
social: Be known by clients as an agency that uses AI well

segments.valueProposition: For small New York professional-services firms that are drowning in repetitive admin, Quillfield Automation finds where AI and automation will save the most hours, builds those workflows on the tools the firm already uses, and keeps them running. A fixed-price audit comes first, so every build starts with a clear business case, and every automation is documented, privacy-reviewed and monitored. Unlike marketplace freelancers, Quillfield stays accountable after launch; unlike large AI consultancies, it works at a price and pace that suits a 10-person firm.

competitors.name: Freelance automation specialists on marketplaces (Upwork, Fiverr)

description.offerings: Zapier, Make and AI chatbot builds, priced by the task or the hour.
description.market: Small businesses across the US and worldwide; any industry.
description.acquisition: Marketplace search, reviews and low hourly rates.
description.experience: Fast and cheap for simple tasks, but quality varies and support often ends when the job does.

competitors.strengths: Low prices; large pool of talent; quick to start.
competitors.weaknesses: Little understanding of professional-services workflows or confidentiality; no ongoing accountability; documentation is rare.
competitors.opportunities: Rising demand for AI automation is pulling more freelancers into the market.
competitors.threats: Marketplace fees and price competition; clients burned by poor builds become wary of all outside help.
competitors.insights: Compete on industry focus, a documented audit, privacy review and a care retainer that keeps automations working, not on hourly rate.

competitors.name: Larger AI consultancies and systems integrators

description.offerings: AI strategy, custom model work and enterprise integrations.
description.market: Mid-size and enterprise firms, often in finance and healthcare.
description.acquisition: Enterprise sales teams, conferences and partnerships with software vendors.
description.experience: Polished and thorough, but slow and expensive for a small firm.

competitors.strengths: Credibility, depth of expertise and large teams.
competitors.weaknesses: Minimum engagements far above a small firm's budget; not interested in 10-person clients.
competitors.threats: Their thought leadership raises expectations of what AI can do.
competitors.insights: Borrow their rigor (audit, roadmap, governance) and package it at a small-firm price with a single accountable person.

competitors.name: DIY no-code and built-in AI tools

description.offerings: Zapier, Make, Microsoft Copilot and AI features inside practice-management software, set up by the firm itself.
description.market: Every small firm with a cloud subscription.
description.acquisition: Free trials, in-app prompts and vendor marketing.
description.experience: Easy to start, but setups stay half-finished and break when nobody owns them.

competitors.strengths: Cheap or already paid for; no outside party involved.
competitors.weaknesses: Needs time and skills the firm does not have; no one to maintain it.
competitors.opportunities: Vendors keep adding AI features, making DIY more tempting.
competitors.threats: Could shrink the market for simple builds.
competitors.insights: Position Quillfield as the partner that makes these tools work together, and offer to maintain what the firm has already started.

competitors.name: Doing it manually or hiring an admin

description.offerings: Staff keep copying data and chasing documents by hand, or the firm hires another administrator.
description.acquisition: No acquisition: it is the default.
description.experience: Familiar and low-risk, but slow, error-prone and costly as the firm grows.

competitors.strengths: No change needed; no new risk; a new hire can also do other tasks.
competitors.weaknesses: An administrator in New York costs $50,000 to $60,000 a year before benefits; manual work does not scale.
competitors.opportunities: A tight hiring market makes the manual route harder.
competitors.threats: Inertia: the pain is spread thinly, so it never feels urgent.
competitors.insights: Show the cost of the status quo in hours and dollars during the audit, and compare the Build and Retainer to the cost of a hire.

offerings.name: AI Workflow Audit
needsAddressed: A clear plan for where AI actually saves time
Hand repetitive admin work to reliable automations

description.function: A fixed-price discovery of how the firm works today, ending in a prioritized automation roadmap.
description.benefit: The firm learns where AI and automation will save the most hours, what it will cost, and what to leave alone.
description.scope: Two interviews, a review of up to eight core workflows and the software stack, a privacy and risk check, and a written roadmap with estimated hours saved and costs. Two to three weeks.
description.delivery: Booked through the website after a free 30-minute call; paid in full upfront by QuickBooks invoice (card or ACH); delivered in a recorded walkthrough and a written report.
description.support: Weekly email updates during the audit; a 30-day follow-up call to answer questions about the roadmap.
description.requirements: Access to one decision-maker and one day-to-day user; read-only access to the tools under review; a signed mutual NDA.

offerings.name: Automation Build
needsAddressed: Hand repetitive admin work to reliable automations
Faster client intake and document handling
Scale delivery without hiring more staff

description.function: Design and build of two to four automations from the audit roadmap, using the firm's own tools plus Make, Zapier and AI models.
description.benefit: Repetitive admin runs on its own, with fewer errors and faster turnaround for clients.
description.scope: Two to four automations, testing with real cases, a privacy review, staff training and written documentation. Four to eight weeks; extra automations quoted separately.
description.delivery: Statement of work and QuickBooks invoice (card or ACH): 50% at signing and 50% on handover about two months later.
description.support: Named point of contact (Jordan); weekly progress call; 30 days of fixes after handover.
description.requirements: A completed audit or equivalent scoping; admin access to the relevant tools; a staff member available for testing.

offerings.name: Automation Care Retainer
needsAddressed: Automations that keep working after launch
Scale delivery without hiring more staff

description.function: Monthly monitoring, fixes and one small improvement to the firm's automations.
description.benefit: Automations keep working as tools and staff change, and keep improving without a new project each time.
description.scope: Error monitoring and alerts, fixes within one business day, AI model and prompt updates, one small improvement a month, and a monthly usage report. Up to six hours a month.
description.delivery: Monthly card or ACH billing through QuickBooks; cancel with 30 days' notice.
description.support: Shared support channel; monthly review call; emergency fixes for failed automations.
description.requirements: An existing Quillfield build or an audited set of automations; continued admin access for monitoring.

value.situation:
We sell AI Workflow Audit ($2,500 a project), Automation Build ($7,500 a project) and Automation Care Retainer ($1,200 a month) to Small professional-services firms in New York City.
Customers find and reach us through LinkedIn, Main Website, Booking / Registration Page, Newsletter, Direct Email, Referral partners (bookkeepers and IT providers), Event / Talk, Invoice and Zoom.
We start with $10,650 in hand and are seeking $15,000 (SBA Microloan). At the normal level we expect $14,250 a month in revenue, breaking even in Jul 2027. The plan still has a funding gap of $16,198.

strengths: Founder with hands-on automation and solutions architecture experience
Three fixed-price services that are easy for a small firm to buy
A Care Retainer that turns one-off projects into recurring revenue
Low fixed costs: a coworking desk and no staff
weaknesses: A single founder's capacity limits how many builds can run at once
The plan relies on an SBA microloan that is not yet confirmed
Cash runs short in mid 2027, even with the loan
No case studies or client track record yet
opportunities: Small professional firms want to use AI but have no one in-house to set it up
Automation platforms keep getting cheaper and more capable
Referrals through accountants and professional associations
Ongoing maintenance demand as firms add more tools
threats: Larger agencies packaging low-cost automation offers for small firms
AI tools that let firms automate on their own, pushing prices down
Stricter privacy and professional-conduct rules on the use of AI
An economic slowdown delaying discretionary projects

value.compass: From 2027 to 2029, Quillfield moves from a solo launch to a stable business with recurring income. Direction: close the funding gap before the mid-2027 low point, then grow the Care Retainer base until recurring revenue covers the fixed costs. Focus: law and accounting firms of 5 to 50 staff in New York City, the three core services, and repeatable, documented builds. What we will not do: build our own software products, take work outside professional services, chase large enterprise contracts or discount to win work.
